sources.title: Proto-Cuneiform Account-Books and Journals
sources.author: Robert K. Englund
sources.authority: Leading specialist synthesis grounded in the archaic tablet corpus and CDLI work.
locators: pp. 24–27 (PDF pp. 2–5), especially chronology figure and discussion of Uruk IV/III corpus
sources.limitations: Chronological ranges and corpus counts reflect the state of publication in 2004; some causal interpretation belongs to WS02.
sources.notes: Supports ca. 3300 BCE emergence, relative Uruk IV→III sequence, overwhelmingly administrative earliest corpus, and caution around token continuity.

sources.title: Uruk and I
sources.author: Hans J. Nissen
sources.authority: CDLI Journal article by a senior Uruk specialist auditing excavation records and chronology.
sources.limitations: Author explicitly foregrounds failures in legacy excavation documentation; exact absolute dates remain model-dependent.
sources.notes: Uruk IVa is the most probable archaeological placement of the oldest script, slightly earlier cannot be excluded; find context is often insufficient and unreliable.

sources.title: Writing in Early Mesopotamia: Beyond the Meme
sources.author: Massimo Maiocchi
sources.authority: Assyriological synthesis focused on early Mesopotamian writing, semiotics and material systems.
locators: pp. 410–412 (PDF pp. 15–17), especially discussion of glottographic/semasiographic boundary
sources.limitations: The chapter advocates a fluid continuum; terminology is analytical rather than a universally accepted threshold definition.
sources.notes: Useful counterweight to a binary true-writing/proto-writing distinction and to a linear token→tablet story.

sources.title: The Origins of Writing
sources.author: Ira Spar
sources.authority: Metropolitan Museum of Art Heilbrunn Timeline essay by a cuneiform specialist.
sources.limitations: Introductory synthesis and now older; statements about possible mid-fourth-millennium Syrian/Turkish systems are provisional.
sources.notes: States that Sumerian identification of Uruk tablets is popular but not universal; phonetic use is sparse before 3000 and consistently apparent much later.

sources.title: Visible Language: Inventions of Writing in the Ancient Middle East and Beyond
sources.author: Christopher Woods (ed.)
sources.authority: University of Chicago Oriental Institute catalogue curated by a Sumerologist.
locators: comparative chronology and essays on earliest Mesopotamian and Egyptian writing; catalogue overview
sources.limitations: Catalogue compresses specialist disagreements for comparative presentation; use for comparison scope, not exact Uruk stratigraphy.
sources.notes: Treats Mesopotamia and Egypt as roughly contemporary independent inventions; supports avoiding an unqualified unique 'world first' claim.

sources.title: Visible Language exhibition overview
sources.author: Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures, University of Chicago
sources.authority: Official ISAC summary of the Woods-curated exhibition.
sources.limitations: Public-facing overview rather than full argument; dates are rounded.
sources.notes: Places Mesopotamian tablets around 3200 BCE and early Egyptian tags around 3320 BCE, illustrating why 'first' depends on definition and dating.

sources.title: The State of Decipherment of Proto-Elamite
sources.author: Robert K. Englund
sources.authority: Corpus-based comparison by a leading proto-cuneiform and proto-Elamite specialist.
sources.limitations: Proto-Elamite comparison is secondary to WS01 and does not establish the spoken language of Uruk scribes.
sources.notes: Supports relative order Uruk IV before Uruk III and contemporaneity/contact with proto-Elamite; shows attribution is regional and transmissional, not a simple ethnic label.

sources.title: The Origins of Writing
sources.author: Metropolitan Museum of Art, object and corpus context
sources.authority: Major museum collection context linked to excavated and collected early tablets.
locators: object description: earliest tablets around 3300 BCE; two early phases
sources.limitations: Single object is illustrative, not representative; provenance and dating of market-derived tablets can be weaker than excavated material.
sources.notes: Material anchor for the approximate 3300 BCE date and phase distinction.
